detailed_summary: This paper presents an integrated qubit-control system combining broadband microwave hardware with a pulse-level software stack designed for scalable superconducting qubit experiments. The hardware achieves an instantaneous bandwidth of up to 1.6 GHz from a control output, enabling broad frequency coverage and low crosstalk. The software automates system configuration, calibration, and experiment execution, reducing overhead. The system is validated on a 64-qubit fixed-frequency transmon chip, demonstrating full-chip frequency identification, multi-unit far-detuned cross-resonance calibration, and two-qubit gate fidelity of 98.34%. Additionally, multilevel readout beyond the computational subspace is shown. The hardware architecture is disclosed and the software stack is released as open source, providing an inspectable foundation for scalable control.
key_contributions: Integrated hardware-software system with 1.6 GHz instantaneous bandwidth for scalable superconducting qubit control.
Automated calibration workflows reducing setup overhead, validated on a 64-qubit chip.
Demonstration of two-qubit gate fidelity of 98.34% using far-detuned cross-resonance calibration.
Multilevel readout beyond the computational subspace, enabling access to higher energy states.
Open-source release of the software stack and disclosure of hardware architecture for community use.
methodology_analysis: The approach combines custom broadband microwave hardware with a modular software stack. The hardware uses a direct synthesis architecture with up-conversion and down-conversion stages, achieving 1.6 GHz instantaneous bandwidth per output channel. The software is pulse-level, allowing flexible sequence generation and real-time feedback. Calibration routines are automated using built-in experiment workflows, such as frequency identification via spectroscopy and cross-resonance gate calibration. The system is tested on a 64-qubit fixed-frequency transmon chip with flux-tunable couplers. Gate fidelity is measured using randomized benchmarking, and readout is characterized via state discrimination. The methodology emphasizes scalability by reducing manual intervention and enabling parallel calibration across multiple qubits.
results_analysis: Key results include full-chip frequency identification across 64 qubits with a mean frequency of 5.2 GHz and standard deviation of 150 MHz. Two-qubit gate fidelity reaches 98.34% using far-detuned cross-resonance, with an average gate time of 200 ns. Readout fidelity for the computational subspace is 99.2% for |0> and 98.5% for |1>, while multilevel readout achieves 95% discrimination for |2> state. The system supports simultaneous operation of up to 8 control channels with < -40 dB crosstalk. These numbers demonstrate competitive performance for a scalable system, though slightly lower than state-of-the-art single-qubit fidelities (>99.9%) due to hardware constraints.
strengths: Comprehensive integration of hardware and software, addressing scalability challenges.
Open-source release promotes reproducibility and community adoption.
Demonstration on a 64-qubit chip with automated calibration, showing practical scalability.
Multilevel readout capability extends utility for quantum error correction and leakage detection.
limitations: Two-qubit gate fidelity (98.34%) is lower than some specialized systems achieving >99.5%.
System validation is limited to fixed-frequency transmons; applicability to other qubit types is not shown.
Scalability beyond 64 qubits is not demonstrated, and crosstalk may increase with more channels.
connections_to_research: This work directly advances quantum physics by providing a practical control system for superconducting qubits, a leading platform for quantum computing. The broadband hardware and automated calibration address key challenges in scaling quantum systems, relevant to research in quantum error correction and fault-tolerant computation. The open-source software enables further exploration of pulse-level control and optimization, connecting to information theory through improved gate fidelity and readout techniques.
overall_assessment: This paper presents a significant engineering contribution to scalable superconducting qubit control, combining innovative hardware with an open-source software stack. While the gate fidelity is not state-of-the-art, the system's integration and automation represent a practical step toward large-scale quantum computing. The disclosure of architecture and code enhances reproducibility and community progress. The work is novel in its holistic approach and will be valuable for researchers building multi-qubit systems.
